story: Joan Miró authored his own poems and created forty color lithographs to illustrate them for the project Le Lézard aux plumes d'or. Published by Louis Broder and printed by Fernand Mourlot in Paris in 1971, the work brought together Miró's writing and printmaking into a single illustrated book. Rather than using lithography to reproduce existing images, he treated the stone directly as a medium for new creation. Through these experiments in printmaking, Miró helped expand the possibilities of twentieth-century art.

In 1967, Joan Miró and his Paris publisher Louis Broder completed printing the first edition of the illustrated book *Le Lézard aux plumes d'or*. Shortly afterward, they discovered an error in the paper stock that distorted the printed lithographs. Because the original lithographic plates had already been erased, the defective edition was destroyed. Miró had to draw an entirely new set of plates, which Broder finally published as the completed edition in 1971.

In 1971, Joan Miró collaborated with the Parisian workshop Atelier Mourlot to print the lithographs for his portfolio *Le Lézard aux plumes d'or*. To launch the presentation of the project at the Berggruen Gallery that same year, Mourlot also printed an original promotional exhibition poster. Two years after Fernand Mourlot's death, the workshop reproduced Miró's 1971 poster design to commemorate the master printer's contribution to the arts.
